projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Basil Crimaldi was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War Two veteran Basil Crimaldi. Mr. Crimaldi served in the US Army with the 35th Division, 320th Regiment. He served in the European Theatre, and he was a prisoner of war. I'm Tom Swope, and this interview was recorded at Mr. Crimaldi's home in Seven Hills, Ohio On July 27, 2004. Basil was 83 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Well, I lived in Cleveland, naturally.

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: __+ I lived in Superior.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you in '41? When were you born?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: I was born in 1921.

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: So I was about 21 or 22 years old. Well, I was drafted when I was 22. I probably was about 21 -- 20 or 20 --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were working in '41? Probably you got a job out of school. Is that right?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Well, my school in -- I spent -- it was in Sicily.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hm.

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: And that's a long story.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You went back to Sicily to go to school?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: It was my parents who went to Sicily. In 1929 my father got a bright idea. He's gonna go over there and live with this -- orchard lemons, oranges, and what have you. So I was only about seven years old when they got first grade here. So I went to high school over there in Sicily.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: And I come back in 1938 -- January 38th. It was hard to get here under Mussolini and all, and I didn't intend to stay there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But you were able to get out of Sicily even though --

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, yeah. They had my name all messed up, but still I worked it out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you went to school from what -- second grade through high school in Sicily?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Yeah, right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Good education, do you think?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Well, they would teach you real quick. They don't waste no time. There's no such a thing as sports and all that stuff. There was just strictly school. Now, today -- I don't know how they work, so I haven't been there since. I swore I never go back. I never did. People ask me "Why don't you want to go back?" Well, what for?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, you weren't born in Sicily? You are were born here?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: I was born here. I was born in Alton, Ohio. This is near Canton -- Akron-Canton Airport. It's not just going -- a little south from there. It was interesting. My father was a brick layer there. Not a brick layer, but a make bricks. It was a big outfit, which they have now in Sugar Creek. Amish country. Those people were German. I think that they owned it. There were Amish people there too. Now it's just a village, and so it's not a bad place.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, was there -- when you were living in Sicily and Mussolini was in power and taking control --

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Oh, yeah --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there a lot of concern about him taking over?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: People couldn't talk. You couldn't say anything; you'll wind up on an island. I don't know what the heck that island -- they call it -- in other words, he doesn't -- he didn't believe in having you executed. But he believed in throwing you there for life. So it was a terrible time. So I had a brother who was trying to make it here -- was my -- he was younger than I was, and he never could make it. I guess he had his passport, but he never could make it because Mussolini kept him over there. He wanted to keep me there, and my oldest brother -- he came here in 1936. He was the oldest. He passed on. Now he's buried up south from here -- can't think of the name of it, and he was in the military too.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, maybe __+

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: No. But they __+ a little later. He was in the 3rd Infantry Division.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But they tried -- he tried to keep you because you were military age? He tried to keep you in Sicily?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Oh, yeah -- yeah. They even give you a uniform every -- from like you have here, boy scouts, but that's a different -- that's a different situation over there. Military style, you know? And he got what he had coming.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Yes, sir. And so, anyway, I came back in 1938. Couldn't speak a word of English. And my brother said to me, you know, to learn the language. I guess -- again you know, you either go to school or go to 3c camp. Civil Conservation Corps. You ever heard of it?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure. Yes.

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Yeah, I was in there. They send us to Nevada from here -- from Cleveland. And there was a beautiful state. Desert. Hot. And from there I spent about -- something about eighteen months in there -- in the Civil Conservation Corps. Dollar a day, and room and board. We had barracks -- they were under the military, but we had __ take us to work building roads out in the desert and drill wells so then we'd have troughs for the stray cows to have water. And it was very interesting for boys, you know, when you're young. You go, go, go and nothing bothers you. But hot as heck. And rattle snakes. And beautiful country. That's about all I can say. From there -- when I got out there around 1940, I think -- '41 or whatever -- I stayed here and got a job in a factory, you know. And I think it was Williard Battery. Probably you heard of it. Maybe not.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think so.

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Yeah. They used to be around St. Claire there -- the east side. And from there I got drafted in '42.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories before that? Do you have specific memories of December 7, 1941?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Oh, yeah. In 1941 I was -- I lived in St. Claire. East 51st, St. Cecilia Church or saint -- something like that. Anyway, I used to hang around that corner because across from there you have a Jewish deli. I used to get corned beef sandwich and a big glass of cherry drink, you know. 35 cents -- pretty reasonable.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hm.

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: And that's when, anyway, one morning -- on a Sunday morning -- I'm standing on the corner and somebody says "You know Japan bombed Hawaii." I just looked, you know. I was stunned. I didn't know what to say, you know. So I was a young boy. I think I was 21 then, around that area, and so that was it. And a lot of them -- I guess they went to the service and got drafted as volunteers. And so I waited for being drafted, because to get into the military those days you had to know how to read and write English, and they give you papers, you know, to fill in a certain amount of time. I couldn't do that. The only thing I could do was sign my name. It was just about what happened when I got drafted and sign my name. If I could understand something I might write it down, and they said to me -- when I got drafted -- they says "How come you don't fill out these papers?" Because I don't know how to fill them out. And "Well, we're gonna have to test you for an IQ and see how good you are." So they had some kind of concoctions and all. They say "You're not dumb. You're pretty smart." You can put them together. I mean -- so I did that, you know, and I got drafted in '42. In '42 I got drafted, yeah. So they say, "You have a pretty high I

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: " They said for a -- I says, "Hey, you know, if you don't have an American education you might have an foreign education." But I never did care for Europe or anything like that so.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were drafted into the army?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Into the army. And I was in the Infantry.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hm. Would that be your first day of training?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: First day of training. That was in Texas. That's where we went to Texas. They call it -- they don't call it Camp Waller now. They call it camp -- Fort Waller. Just like when we wind up in Alabama. They'll call it Camp Rucker. And they call it --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- Fort Rucker.

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Fort Rucker. That's near Ozark, Alabama. I even got married there. Idiot. At 22 getting married. That was the dumbest thing I ever did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. And shortly after you got into the army you got married?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Yeah, about a year later. I said to myself, "Wow __." When you come to think -- you have no brains when you're at that age. So anyway from Texas we had our basic training. Run mineral wells __+. If you've ever heard, many people used to go there during the depression, you know, about their water. Whatever that was. So from Texas, after we had our basic training, we went to California. And this was -- this place they call it something like Ohio, but it isn't spelled Ohio like O-JI-O or --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, Ojai. I use to live in California. I think it's O-J-A-I.

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Yeah, beautiful place. But we're there during the winter. When we left Texas and got into California -- and wow -- hot as hell in this weather -- in the desert part of it, you know. As we get into the city, it's just as hot. We wind up over there at this place -- we stayed there about -- during the winter. It started to rain around January. It never stopped raining -- every day, every day. So for about a month, or almost 2 months, so we said "well, we're gonna pack up and we're gonna leave and go east." So wind up in Alabama. So that's where we had our really basic training. So we used to train over there. We were more like an advanced training -- our company was. Anyway they walk us twenty-five miles a day every day for eight and a half months. Unbelievable. Now I can't even walk a half a mile. God, the stamina we had.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you assigned to an outfit at that point?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Pardon me?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you assigned to an outfit?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Yeah, well, we were assigned in O-JI or --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Ojai.

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Ojai or whatever they want to call it. I was assigned with an outfit. It was a national guard from Nebraska. One-hundred and thirty-four they call her. One hundred and thirty-four Battalion or, you know. And I was training with them and then they -- what they did they formed another. They called it a 320. When we got to Alabama they formed a 320 and they needed a good man so they picked me, and a few others, and they put us with these new rookies. That's how they formed the 320 because they had 134,137 and 320 and, gee, I was so disappointed, you know, but then I got used to it. We had a lot of southern boys from Tennessee, Kentucky, and North Carolina. These guys were really funny. They were really funny. A good bunch of boys. And we had our training there, and they sent us to Europe.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your job at that point when you were being trained?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: I was a PFC.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: PFC Rifleman?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Rifleman. That was my job -- Rifleman, yeah. They'd try you with everything, I mean, to get me familiar with all the equipment whatever you -- I don't care if it was a motor or a Rifleman or a machine gun -- everything. So good Infantry, man. Well, there were a lot of boys which didn't have no education. I was one of them. A lot of southerners, and some of them did have an education. And so the best thing for you would be the Infantry. See, I couldn't get into anything else, and I would have liked to have been to some different outfit or whatever. But it was okay. I was happy. So from there we went to Europe.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you in Alabama? Is that when you got married?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Yeah. Ozark Alabama.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And married your high school or --

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: No, no. Just a --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- A girl back home?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Just a nice lady. She came down there -- we got married over there with the justice of the peace and had a couple of buddies there. They were -- what do you call it -- best man and all that stuff, you know. And that was foolish. I mean, a marriage, it's okay. But you have to use your head and think.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it the old thing of "I want to get married because I don't know if I'm coming back?" That sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Something in that way, you know. So then my wife, before she went home, she came back to Cleveland. She announced she got pregnant, and like you say, if you don't know if you're gonna come back or not. So she named my son Basil, like me. And I said "What did you do that for?" She says "Well, maybe you won't come back. At least I have a Basil."

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: I says "Oh, gee." So.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not what you wanted to hear, probably.

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: No. So from there we went to Europe.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When was that? When did you go to Europe?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: No. Early '44.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Early '44.

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Right. Because then we went to Normandy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was that crossing like in '44?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: How was it?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The Atlantic crossing. What was that like?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: It wasn't too bad because we heard too many of these ships were getting knocked off, and we started off from New York in the dark. By daylight there must have been over 300 ships. Where in the heck did they come from? And the German subs -- they were afraid to get tangled up with us because they had the __+ and everything else and aircraft carrier and, you know. I went up there to Europe -- an old German ship from the 411 they told us. So then we landed in Liverpool. Cobblestone Road. It's really an ancient city. Unbelievable. And from there they took us to Exeter. It's more on the -- the other side of the island, you know. Liverpool is more like in the east, and this is more like in the west. Exeter -- beautiful country. They -- that's all they like -- is all this glass and stuff. Really beautiful. So we stayed at that thing about three months and we were getting ready to go to Normandy. I'm glad I wasn't in the first wave because, you know, a lot of them got killed there. Because when they went to land they couldn't land it right at the beach; they would land way before the beach because they all -- this cross __+ they were walled up together -- in the beach area -- so we landed there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How early did you go in? When did you go in?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: In Normandy?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you land? Right.

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: We landed exactly one month later.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hm.

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: The invasion started June 6th, and we landed at -- July the 6th. And that was short and sweet, I'll tell you, because I got captured. So everything was a mess. But when we landed over there, you know, we couldn't land to the beach. And after a month later still the beach was -- you couldn't clear it away, I guess. So when we landed some guys fired down, I mean, to touch the ground. Some could swim, some couldn't swim. That makes it kind of rough. I was always a swimmer. In the mean time, the __ swimmer and the pack holds you up in the water. And so the one to the beach was nothing there yet. But when they made the invasion there was really a mess. And I see those -- we call them pill box -- which they were fortified with the Germans, and they had them. They sure had them on that beach.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What beach was that? Was that Omaha?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Omaha beach.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was Omaha?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Omaha beach, yeah. I see that so many times on TV.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hm.

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: And from there they said to us they're still not to too far inland -- about six miles or so. That close they can send the artillery out into the beach. So then we walked up. We were all soaking wet with our salt water. Oh, geez. And so I spent about a good month before I got captured. In other words, I got captured on August 11th. That's just about three days -- four days -- after a month. That's short and sweet.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first day in combat?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Well, when we first went there we set our -- set up a place near __. That's in France, naturally. And the first thing we did -- we made a slick trench enough to cover so you're not above the ground, and we set up and we stayed over there. Well, we keep moving around from time to time. Really a lot of combat I didn't see, but I saw some of that where you thought you'd never make it. These guys, when they'd zero in on you -- those 88s -- they really hammer you real good. So you stay low. So the only thing they get you with is the shrapnel. If it lands on you, or if you get a direct hit, forget it. The first thing -- when we started -- we advance and before you know it all hell broke loose. And you were really scared, I'm telling you. You're really scared. Especially when you see your own officer -- lieutenant -- he got direct hit and his body was hanging on a tree. And when you see that, and you see skulls, you know, that's really scary. But you keep going. You follow the gang. So from there, I don't know about -- we saw quite a bit in a month's time. But it don't seem like it, but we did see a lot of combat, you know. One thing I like when they were going -- we're gonna go up that hill -- but first we're gonna chop that hill down first. Between bombing and artillery, I said, "That's the way to do it. That's the way to fight." But sometimes they goof up, because I see some wrong things that I don't like. So we was supposed to go on that hill, and we had an Indian boy. A Native American. He was loaded. He had a hold of a cognac, and he was so loaded that we kept him in a foxhole. There he said "Don't ever turn this boy into the lieutenant," or something like that. Because he'll get court marshaled. So we went on top of the hill, and that's when we went and slept for the whole night. And we slept on top of that hill, and the Germans were gone out of there. That's one thing. So the next day, when daylight came around, that fellow -- he was all right. This Native Indian -- this Native American -- whatever. So everything was okay. And for where we went from there -- we never made St. Lowell. Because there was another outfit there, and they heard that they bombed the hell out of the Americans. Bombed the heck out of our poor soldiers. Sometimes it's hard to remember all that. So anyway, we stayed in one spot there for awhile. We were moving around, but not advancing as fast as we thought we would. But I think after that we did. They came around with this tank where they could come over the hedges. Hedgerow -- hedgerow. You'd figure just a hedge, you know. These were mounds of dirt that separated property. They have a lot of orchards there. Apples. And so they put, like, two forks in the front of the tank. And the tank digs into the ground and pulls right through and makes a big path. You've probably seen it on TV.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hm.

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: It was unbelievable. The Germans saw that, they really got scared. But anybody's scared. Afraid one is in the war. Anyway, so from there -- one day the lieutenant says "Well, we're gonna get in the tanks and we're gonna break the lines." I says, "Uh-oh." That scares you. You're a sitting duck on the tank. And we had small tanks. When you see those tanks, compared to ours now. I understand now we have good tanks. Huge. Now I hear they have this one tank, you can hit it, and you still won't kill the guys inside it. That's something. So okay. We're traveling along the road. We went through the enemy lines, and we parked. We stopped up there. First we got ?pop-shots? from the Germans. ?Burp gum? they called it. We used to call it. And they turned the gun towards them. They quiet down, so we parked ourselves there for awhile. And you could hear a big, huge tank. Click, click, click, click. A German tank. These are the Tiger tank. And so we stayed there shooting all night long. And we saw -- say, what do you call it -- coming down the road. Our own Jeep. The Germans had it. They had a habit of using our own equipment. So when they called for a bazooka, we knocked that out real quick. But after that -- okay, we stayed over there. We usually would draw when dark comes around. We used to do it every night. I used to go on night patrol myself. You know, every night. Because I figure they can't see me, they can't shoot me. I use to volunteer -- I was a crazy boy to volunteer this night patrol. I almost shot a horse. It was facing direct to us -- I thought it was a soldier. Then as he turns around, it was a horse. That was funny. And you do not want to shoot because you don't want to give your position away, wherever you're located. And so okay, we parked over there for overnight and I said "Gee, I guess we're gonna stay here." This fellow, he just got in the service. I'm not in the service __+ in combat. Eighteen years old. I'm already twenty-four. And so okay. Daylight came around, we looked around, there's nobody there. This kid says "What are we gonna do now?" I says "We stay put." What else can you do? We know the Germans were on the one side in front of us, if they're still there, I don't know. But I know this: one tank was on our left, camouflaged, because he just knocked out one of our tank. An 88 went over our head, and it hit that tank -- our tank. I hope nobody was in there -- I don't remember. I don't know what happened after that. This was located in Marten The town of ?Marten? I don't know if you've ever heard of it. In France.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: M-A-R-T-E-N?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Yeah, something like that, you know. In France. Normandy. In other words, it's a beautiful area there. And so we waited and waited. And you couldn't move because you don't know which way to go. When we didn't see our outfit over there, they usually they say "Hey, we're gonna move now." They'll pat you on the side of the back or whatever and we'll move out. But nobody said anything, so that's how we got captured. We looked around, sit there a while, before you know it the Germans are coming -- not only in the front, they were behind us. And the kid said "What are we gonna do?" And I said "I'll tell ya. The only thing we can do is hope and pray they don't see us." But they spotted us. So now there was a little mud there, like a ditch. We'll just put our rifles right there because you can't fight these guys. Just you and I. So we throw our rifles in the mud, and they stomped on them, and that's it. And they saw us with the rifles and they went like this -- put you're hands up -- so we put our hands up. The first thing, we got rid of our helmets, because we had that net cap underneath of us. And that was it. This -- this happened August 11. And from then on it took us into the -- well, first thing this German sergeant says "Don't try to escape see? These boys, these SS, they'll shoot you on the spot. If I wasn't here they would shoot you right now." Fanatic boys. Smoked like hell. I don't know if they were smoking pot. Who knows. So hey, a war is a war. So this sergeant, he had a couple of guys take us into a mansion. Wow. A French mansion. What a place. Furniture like you won't believe. High class place. And there were the German officers over there, and the first thing they said was "You hungry? I'll give you --." Hungry? Well, gee. How can you be hungry? You're nervous as hell. I'm still nervous. So they gave us potatoes. They're good at potatoes, you know. The Germans eat a lot of potatoes and cabbage. And it tasted pretty good. But you can't compare it to what we used to eat. So we were there, and they didn't say anything. They just sent us from there -- before we left there a few more guys got captured. Before you know it there were forty of us. Not just from my outfit -- from different outfit. And there were forty of us all together. So okay. They took us from there. Everything was walking and walking, and one place we were walking and here comes these Germans. We're on the road and here comes a P38 straight -- a P51 or P38 -- straight for those Germans. And they got this German fellow in the neck here, and you know, he was crying like a baby. And I don't think he made it. So they look at us and I says -- the one guy says, "Oh, god I hope they don't kill us now." So they let us go. So from there they took us to -- it was around this Marten -- this town. And we stayed at an overnight, about forty of us all together. We even had a Chaplain. And I guess -- I don't know if he was Jewish or German American -- German, in other words. And they spoke German. So we stayed there overnight in this building. They kept us over there, but the next day I don't know what they were gonna do. But anyway, we stayed over there and one by one these guys were leaving, these guards, and I said "Geez, what's with this?" We couldn't figure that out. So when no guards were there he said, the last guy says, "I'll be back" You know, "Don't move. You stay here." He never came back. We waited. One of the guys, the Chaplain, says "Let's get out of here." So we moved away from there, and we saw a barn. And this barn -- we walked in there. There was nobody in there, but there was a house not too far. And we __+, wouldn't you know, the French people they turned us in. But we couldn't understand that, you know. Why, if they were to get caught -- if the Germans would have caught those French -- not telling them-- they would have killed them. So we'll put two and two together. That's the thing. So before you know it we saw a bunch of Germans coming up with a Colonel, you know. He says __+ "What's going on?" And this fellow says "Let me talk," because he spoke German, this Chaplain. And he says "Well, we're waiting for the guards. They told us to wait here." Which -- they told us to wait in the other place -- not this place. And the Americans weren't too far from there, but we just couldn't get away. Just couldn't get away. And from there they moved us around, sometimes with trucks. One night they put us in the trucks. Okay. And they stop on one road, I don't know where. It still had to be Normandy. And so here comes our artillery hammering away. God, we almost got killed by our own artillery. We'd be in the truck sitting still and the artillery going. Oh, uh-oh. We're gonna get hit. It goes right over the top and explodes right there. Now our artillery was powerful. It would make a hell of a big hole, I'll tell ya. And so finally they moved out of there. And from there they took us somewhere, I don't know where. And, like I said, there were a good forty of us and they marched us for quite awhile until we got to Paris. Paris was a beautiful city. Us guys are right away looking at the women. Forget the women, man. I'm worried about my life. So from there they finally decided -- after they walk us quite a few days walking -- and we could out-walk those Germans compared to -- I used to walk twenty-five miles a day. Walking was nothing to me. It was a picnic. So from there they put us in boxcars like a bunch of cattles. I said, "I don't know where the hell we're going now." But you figure they might take us to Germany. Which they did. And they pack us in there like you won't believe. They give us a can there and he says, "That's your toilet." And no eat. No food and no drink. So as we're driving along in a railroad car, we wind up in Frankfurt, Germany. Somebody says "This is Frankfurt." We looked; there was a prairie. Everything was flattened. It was an industry place. Frankfurt. It was flattened. So this was around twelve o' clock. And so we heard a siren. Uh-oh. So the train pulled away from the center of Frankfurt. Moved away -- more away from the city. And they were bombing the hell out of -- boxcars were shaking from bombing the city. And the way our boxcar was shaking -- there was one kid -- I thought he was going to go crazy. Screaming and hollering. "See what they did?" The Germans -- they went away from there. There was a wooded area. They went there, and they left us over there. And we were hoping they won't strafe us. I heard later round that anything goes in Germany. And they know they're a prisoner of war -- they could be a prisoner of war -- and they didn't strafe us or bombed us. We were lucky. So that was what was scary. Really scary. When the United States bombed and everything, especially the railroad, they're like you wouldn't believe. They clean up. From there we went to Munich. A beautiful city. Not quite touched yet. Not quite touched. And we went to -- from there-- might have been maybe thirty or thirty-five miles. They call it Moosberg. This small town. I guess that's where they were stationed, in Moosberg. Stalag -- seven, eight -- and we stayed over there. I was over there for eight and a half months. So I didn't see too much combat, but I seen enough. I know one time we were trying to take over to help out this other outfit. We almost got chopped down. I mean, from there totally, those 88s were pouring like rain. And I see those guys getting hit, and I look at myself. And gee, how come I didn't get hit? I was full of that black dirt, you know, from the explosion and everything like that. There was another incident that -- as we're walking along there was a wagon. Two horses and a wagon. They were carrying, I don't know, supplies. Because they had a lot of that. The Germans. They carry -- they had -- they were getting short on trucks or whatever. There were -- so they had this truck, this wagon, with two horses pulling it. And here comes a P38. Not 38 -- a thunderbolt. A P47 coming down. Uh-oh. We all ran away from the road and there was a lot of orchards, like I said before, apples and everything. We ran away, and before they strafe like hell, and then they drop the bomb. And we were away from the road. I was laying here under this apple tree. Before you know it, this bomb exploded. My body was like -- {four thuds in the background} -- you bounce off, I bet, six inches at least from the concussion. And then all of a sudden, all those apples are falling all over me. I don't know what the hell is happening. So there was part, before you even got to the railroad, you know, getting loaded in these box cars. So anyway, from there -- like I said -- they took us to Moosberg. And that settled everything. And there was a Captain there. He was from the First World War. I forgot his name. You talk about a gentleman. I can say about this guy -- he was a good man. He was from the Second World War, and we were under regular army. No SS. And that made it fine for us but. Doesn't mean we had food or anything like that, you know. So he told us -- he came out there. We're all lined up. And he says, "I know it's the duty for a POW -- a prisoner of war or whatever -- to escape," but he says, "My advice is don't." He said "They catch you out there, they'll shoot you. You'll never come back. You'll never make it. Your best bet you wanna survive is just to stay put." There was a lot of them that tried it, but I don't know what happened. But you see, we didn't talk about trying to escape. Because if anybody were to escape, they only talk to their own buddies. I wasn't their buddy. I was a buddy of this group, so they didn't trust anybody. I can understand that. So when we were over there we had French, we had English, we had all the nationalities in the world. They were all there. Unbelievable. By the time -- at the end of April -- when we got liberated by Patton, somebody said to me there must have been seventy thousand. That's a lot of POWs over there. There were most of them from the Air Force. They had fellows from France -- germ -- I mean, these French soldiers been there for five years. This one fellow -- stranger -- said "This is my wife." She didn't have no clothes on, and I says "Your wife? And you're showing her to me and these guys?" What's the matter with these guys, you know? It was unbelievable. So okay. We went along with it. That's your life. And so we stayed there for eight and a half months. That was strange for us; nobody would do that. But starvation like you wouldn't believe. They'd give us one slice of bread a day. It would be, I would say, maybe five eighths of an inch thick. But this bread was solid. I mean, heavy, dark. And somebody would say they put sawdust in there, this and that, but I don't care. I know it was wheat. That much I know. And it tasted good, because they have anything else to eat and that bread wouldn't go no where. For a young man, the way when you're young, you eat like crazy. Anyway, then they would give us one potato, one slice of bread. The potato, if it's rotten, too bad. You either eat it or throw it away. And naturally you couldn't eat it. And they would give us a little cabbage -- blue cabbage -- dirty cabbage soup. It was filthy. I mean, you had to have the sand and everything settle down before you could eat it. There wasn't very much anyway, and that was our meals. A __ would come up in the evening sometime. They saved the tea for everybody with a big pop. You had to take it, but you wouldn't drink it because some kind of herb. You figure you're thirsty or whatever, you drink that stuff, before you know it in the middle of the night you wet yourself without even knowing it. When that happened to me I never touched that anymore. But never give them a full pop back because then they won't give you anything. So we used to dump it in the sewer there, and they give them the empty pop. We had to learn all the tricks that they were doing to us. We had to learn their tricks. In other words, how to get around them. So it went on and on and on. Then one day they were looking for shoemakers, or schuster, they called them. And the schneider is a tailor. And one guy says "Yeah, I'm a tailor." Tailor of what? So I tell him, "Well, I'm a shoemaker trying to get away from going downtown in Munich, filling in these bomb holes and the railroad tracks and all that stuff." So I worked there for awhile. Actually, making these wood sole, you know -- you ever see these Dutch shoes? You know, they used to be whole bottom wood and we would just put the -- what do you call it -- over the top. Canvas, it looked like. And nailed it around and you got yourself a shoe. And we were wearing those. Clunk, clunk. What a mess. And it was cold as hell. And we would go down Munich, fill in these bomb holes. And one day it was around noon hour, and they had a raid. And I said, "Gee, in daylight?" Oh, yeah, yeah. The Americans bomb every day, and they really started hammering Munich. But they would hit the railroad track. The English would come at night with the mosquito or whatever they were, and drop this thousand pound blockbuster. Oh, man. They'd drop one right where the people live. The next day, when we went there, if it wasn't for the guards those civilians would have killed us, you know. Unbelievable. So we never went back there anymore. And they really used to protect us. As much as they hate us they would protect you. Because a couple of time you got hit with the butt of a rifle, you know. This Jewish boy you know, he was cold. We had a fire there okay. Half a dozen __+ and a half a dozen by the fire. We changed shifts. That Jewish boy, he wasn't used to it. He was from New York, and he says "I'll take your turn." I says, You take it easy." Because I was really tough then, I was. And so he was really frozen this poor boy. So was I. I froze many times -- my feet. So I was more hardier than he was, but still, when it's cold, it's cold. And so one day we're standing there by one of these big holes you know, and here comes an officer. He grabs a hold of the rifle, the soldier -- the soldier -- and starts swinging at us. Hitting us. Because he wonders what are we doing standing -- fill this hole up -- you know. I understand. And good thing he didn't get to me because, man oh, life, the way he was swinging that rifle. It not only hurts you, it can break your back or your hip or anything like that. I know. I got hit a couple of times here, you know, with the butt of the rifle. That's just what they wanted to do I guess. And we used to trade cigarettes. I didn't smoke. I never smoked my whole life. And we used to get a package for four guys from the Red Cross, then it went down to about six then it went down to eight. And he got nothing. So I used to take the cigarettes. I says when, in the morning when we go to Munich, we trade them for bread. And that's what helped us. Trading a cigarette for bread.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Trading with the --

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: -- with the Germans. With the people. Because they all want to smoke. Actually, I traded once with an Indian fellow. These are -- what the hell you call it -- they from India. They fought with the English. They were prisoners of war. He would give me Spam and I would give him a package of cigarette. Man, one day I was so hungry I ate the whole thing. And I said, "Oh, no more." I got sick like you won't believe. So these fellows, you know. One day I had shoe polish, and we stopped at one of the restaurants. And I said to this girl giving me bread -- she grabbed that shoe polish and took off -- I said, "Hey, hey." The guard says "She'll be back." She come back and she gave me two loaves of bread. All this bread, we used to take it to camp so people could eat.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The guards knew you were doing that?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They did?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: You'll give them cigarettes. There you are.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Bribe them a little bit.

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: But sometimes -- yes. You know, I never done this in my life because I'm an honest person. I don't believe in that. But you had to do it because of hunger. When you're hungry you'll take anything, you know. And ever since then, if I see anybody hungry, I'll feed them. Because hunger is the worst thing. You become almost like an animal. And so --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: [audio is cut off] . . . War news much in that camp?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We used to get the news. We used to get the news from -- I don't know who used to pick it up. But like I say, everything was secret. You don't wanna ask questions either. Just let it go. So they used to tell us all about how far they were, and all that stuff. Because by the end of it -- wasn't quite the end of April. Something around the 20th. Somewhere around there Patton came in; and they even told us that they were close. Patton came in there with a jeep, and a driver, naturally. And he -- it wasn't the first time I saw him. I saw him in England. Eisenhower, Patton, and Bradley before we left for Normandy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where was that?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: In Exeter. And then I saw Patton after that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did he address the troops in Exeter?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: From Exeter we went to Plymouth. That's where we got the ship to cross the channel.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But you saw the three of them? They said farewell to the troops?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, yeah. Eisenhower shakes hands with the troop guys. He goes down the line. He said "Remember I'm going home." That means take care of yourself over there so you can go home too. When he said he's going home I said to myself "Yeah, you're going home. But I don't know if I am." But thank the good lord I'm here. Yeah, I'm 83 years old, and so I keep on going and so --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What do you remember about that day of liberation?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: When they liberated me?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When __ was liberated. Right.

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Well, before they liberated us there was a lot of firing going on. There were SS that came into the camp. They wanted to take over, so the regular army, they took care of us. They fought it out between the SS and the regular army. Germany -- they were fighting against each other, you know. We had a wonderful Captain. German Captain from the Second World War. So I stayed inside because those stray bullets, they'll get you. So I stayed against a wall and down low, and that was it. You talk about shaking like a leaf. You won't believe it. You had nothing to protect yourself. And so when Patton came in and the Captain -- that thing he gave him -- his pistol, and he had, you know, all those other guards. They gave up so many -- one good thing, I'd say, they kept those SS out of there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you think the SS were plotting to execute --

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: -- Oh, yeah --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- Did away with the prisoners?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Whatever they do they did it in the Battle of the Bulge. They'd kill a lot of them, and for no reason even. If you can't feed them, don't kill them, you know. Those SS were really rotten. Because I know. I heard when they took Berlin, the Russians -- they lost sixty thousand men. Sixty thousand just in the city of Berlin. I think that's a lot of men. So they really fight for their country. A lot of them gave up, but a lot of them -- most of them -- they fought for their country. So anyway, Patton was there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did he address the prisoners when he came? Did he talk to them?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Yeah, he just said a few words. I even forget what he said. He was standing in the Jeep. He was a big man, I'll tell you. Two pistol. I said, "Yep, just the way they say it," you know. I saw him over there __+ with the two pistols in England. And so he was over there, you know. He was -- he liked war. Patton liked war. Eisenhower was not too keen. It was a different situation -- different thinking, you know. So anyway, from there we got liberated and they put us in a C47 transport plane. They had a little airport over there, and they put us over there, and the next day you drop all your clothes -- your dirty, filthy, blankets, you know. You talk about filth. They used to give us a shower about once every two weeks. They sent us through a shower, then they'd get your clothing to put it in the licen, you know. Some kind of chemical. Smells like hell, but you put them on anyway. You figure -- hey, better than nothing, you know. So that's what went on. Starvation, starvation. And so -- but they -- one thing they took care of us. They used to have there an area. Well, they had a lot of Russians and a lot of Ukrainian people. And they separated them from them the Russians. They had a bunch of Russians; they had TB __+. And there was one compound. They kept them away from everybody, the ones with the TB. Every day they pull them out -- dying, you know. It was a terrible thing. You see so many stories on TV and stuff like that. It was just unbelievable. I couldn't watch them before, and now -- gradually -- sometimes I'll watch them for a little bit, and I'll shift channels. And from there we went to -- anyway, they put us in these C47 planes. And I never fly. I never fly. It was the first time and the last time. And my family's like "How come you don't fly?" I don't fly. So these C47 had lined up there. One takes off just before the next plane was -- mine pull up, you know. This one's made of flip. Wouldn't you know, the darn thing exploded. Went on fire. Oh, geez, you know. You see that again. And anyway. So okay. You follow the next. We took the next plane and I said, "Gee, I can't stay awake." So I lay down on the floor of the plane and I went to sleep, you know. Before we're getting off the -- guy's "Hey, buddy." I don't know who it was. Anyway, everybody's buddy. And he says, "We're getting down." You know, "We're gonna land." And this was a Lucky Strike camp -- you've probably heard of that. And we landed over there. A lot of tents. And when we landed there were a lot of these Red Cross girls. I feel bad about it because I wasn't paying too much attention. I didn't want anything, you know. They wanna give -- I don't know if -- well, they wanna give me something. I don't know what it was -- for coming back -- for landing over there in the Lucky Strike. And I ignored them, and that wasn't me. And it still hurts me. So anyway, they gave us a place -- take your pick -- whatever tent you want to sleep you'll sleep in it. So they gave us clothes. We showered up and shaved and new uniforms. It was fine. Clean clothes, anyway. So we went out. They're gonna feed us, you know. Three times a day. So we went for the first meal. Oh, it looked so good. You're eating like crazy. They had a lot of these vitamin pills in a bowl; take them if you wanna take one. At least I used to take three or four. I think that was wrong. I didn't know what I was doing. So no sooner I got through eating I got nauseated. So I run to the tent over there and I lay down there to sleep it off -- that's the only way I could gradually get back to myself. So until the day came and they took us to the states -- took Lahar . Took a ship there. And we came to the states. And then they were saying -- a lot of these guys -- they told us "If you see any souvenirs -- if you want a pistol." Stuff like that. I didn't want nothing to do with souvenirs. I could have had a duffel bag full of these Lugers. I didn't want nothing. Even today, I don't own a gun. I don't want nothing to do with that. Nothing. See, I always felt, you know, everybody wants to live. What a gun does -- it kills people. It is up to the person. And ever since then, I never would want a rifle or a gun or a shotgun. My father did. He had two pistols and two shotgun. But I was different than my father. And from there we came to the states. And we were lined up over here in New York, and we went to a routine -- whatever, checkup, and all that stuff. And from there they sent us to -- first they sent us home and told us to go to Miami beach.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you got off the boat? What was that like when you finally got to see them?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Well, I got to see my wife, anyway. And my aunt. Because my parents lived there in Europe -- and they died there -- and I never got to see them. So I was unhappy. I was disappointed. I don't know why, I just wasn't happy. And so I went on from there, and maybe was more nervous all the time. Even my aunt says, "You're not the same. You're very nervous. If I was you, I'd go to the V.A." I never did. I used to go to work -- I got a job. I went to work, and that was it. Then I finally -- about 25 years now -- I started going to the V.A. And I get my benefits or whatever it is. But I was just a very unhappy person. I just can't figure out why; I can't explain it. I was married. I tried to take care of my family. Then I had a girl -- a boy and a girl. And she got a nervous breakdown, and she took her own life. And so then I had people take care of my kids while I go to work. I got married a second time -- and when she took her own life I was 35 years old. And then I got married when I was -- three, four, years later -- I got remarried. Because one old woman, she said, "Now, you marry that woman. She likes kids. She never been married." I says, "I don't know. Maybe I'm taking a chance." "No, go ahead." And she was a wonderful woman. Seventeen years later she dies from cancer in the stomach. I said, Gee, that's the kind of luck I have." But, all in all, my whole life I've been very unhappy. But I always smile to people, and keep on going. Keep on doing whatever. And so that's the kind of life I've been doing. I live here alone, and have a friend. I've known her now -- after my wife passed away -- now I've known her -- in November it will be 27 years. And this woman is about seven years older than me -- almost 8 -- and she is 90 years old. A nice person. Just to talk to somebody. Just really friendly. And people wonder "How did you meet somebody, and you stay with this woman?" Hey, it gets to the point where you have to talk to somebody. And you have to have a friend. So it's been that way. But there's so much more to tell that you can't remember everything. You can't remember everything.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, you mentioned getting parcels from the Captain. Did you get much mail from home?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: No. Never. Got a -- they told me -- my ex said to me "I sent you packages and sent you letters." But I never received them. The Germans, they kept them. And like I said before, about these packages, it was supposed to be the Red Cross send you -- they found warehouses full of Red Cross packages. There was about -- they might have been twelve by twelve or about four inches high -- and there was supposed to be one for each person a week. And that would be sufficient. But one guy said, "We cannot feed you that way because you get ideas you might want to escape on a full stomach." So there was a saying and a thinking that way. So what do you do? But I didn't get anything. She found out later, my wife, that I was captured.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long was it before she found out that you were captured?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Oh, I really don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But she probably got a missing in action telegram?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Yeah, missing in action. That's about all she had after she found out. Later, it might have been three or four months before she found out. And so, I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any particularly close buddies either in the army before you were captured or in the camp?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Friends -- more like -- sort of a buddy, yeah. I even had one fellow in the camp when I was a prisoner of war. He was from California. He was Spanish person. Actually, in California they had a lot of Spanish people. And we were buddy-buddy with him. Together we used to share things, you know. And when I was in the camp here -- when I was in the military -- was with these three fellows that were here. First one that actually went out was in the hundred and thirty-four. I had ?Joe Strain? and they both died. I think they were from Toledo. Joe strain and Cliff Voyaga was to be three of us. We used to go out together all the time. I wasn't a loner, really. And we used to be buddy-buddy, all three of us. They both had a wife, and finally I got married. And actually, they came to visit me in Cleveland and I went to visit them in Toledo. Then when they separated us and formed the 320 I met this ?Bright, Rise, and Cook? . Cook was really calmer, because he was just barely speaking southern. He was from the mountain, but he was the nicest guy him, and you know, southerners. They were my buddy, three of them. Another one was from Kentucky. Sartan they used to call him. Well, and he was funny. He was really funny. He was a big, tall guy. Clumsy. But nice people. Nice people. I I found the south was beautiful. I was in maneuvers in Tennessee -- maneuvers. And I thought they were the most wonderful people I had ever met. They would knock down those fences, and naturally the government would replace them. And one day, you know, it was early morning. It was cold as a son of a gun. We were doing maneuvers during the winter. It was cold -- snowing and everything. We saw a barn -- a house. First it was a barn, then we saw this house. There were three of us; I don't even remember who they were anymore. And he says, you know, we'll try to see if we can get hot biscuit and country sausage with eggs. We went there, knocked on the door. There were a bunch of southerners sitting in there. These older ones, you know. And I asked the woman if she would make us some hot biscuits and bacon and eggs and home fries. "Oh, sure. Why not?" So she made it. There were three of us. And we got through with it and the guys say, "Gee, I don't have no money." And I said, "Oh, Basil." You know. And so I gave the lady twelve dollar. She didn't want it. "No, no, no -- you take it." At that time twelve dollars was, you know, a lot of money. But I gave her twelve dollar. But while we were there in Tennessee maneuvers they would have a lot of these poor people. They would have chickens, you know. I'm trying pull out my napkin. That's what I'm trying to do.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: There we go.

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: You'll get it, then you don't have it. See I lost my feelings in my fingers. I had carpal tunnel. They would go down to these farms, you know. They had eggs. All you can eat. I ate so many eggs, and a dummy, we used to put them in our helmet to boil them. You know, so we got to have a hard-boiled egg. It got to the point I was sick of them. So I said, "That's it. Cut it out." You know, we were getting our meals, but why would you want more eggs? I mean, hungry, young -- you can eat like you won't believe. Now if I have a half a sandwich I'm full. I can't believe it. But that's the way it is, you know. I had friends. I had buddies. Oh, yeah -- actually, my Sergeant -- he was a PFC like I was. By the time I got -- before I got -- even -- I was in the states. What they did -- they made a Corporal out of me. They said, "This came from Washington. You're a Corporal now." Okay. And my friend -- this one here -- Stanley King -- Stanley, something like that. Stanley King or whatever. He was from the state of Washington. He was my staff sergeant and squad leader, and when we were in combat we were buddy-buddy. But then, you know, everybody on their own. You watch yourself and that was it. And I had him as a friend. Really a good friend for a sergeant. So we got along real good.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: In the camp were you able to do anything for entertainment or anything to pass the time?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Well, in the camp they used to have the guys play a show. We had a fellow from New York -- he could sing almost like Bing Crosby. And this was around Christmas time so he sung "White Christmas," you know. And he was really good. Then they had one fellow here who was an American. And he was thin, and he would dress like a woman. That's one thing I can't stand -- when somebody's going to dress like a woman. I said, "I understand. I've seen it," you know. But that wasn't my taste. And he used to get these guys really excited. That's unbelievable, you know. So they'd have little shows for us, and you kept yourself busy doing things. And if you were a Catholic they -- well, these guys say the rosary every night. And you better be honest because they'll give you -- they had that ?kangaroo cord? . They whipped the hell out of one boy. But I could feel his whipping.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did he do?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: I don't know. He stole food or something like that. And you can't do that. What's yours is yours, and his is his. And that's it. And the ?kangaroo cord? is terrible. Boy, I didn't know what the heck that was. So we had all different kinds of entertainment. We had some of these guys from England too. They were really showmen, you know. And then we had people from Poland when they had the sixty days riot -- when they chased the Germans out of Warsaw. And they had clarinet player. They had a tenor from the -- violin -- this fellow was a violin. He had long hair. He was an old fop . And they had all the instruments with them. And they were from the house -- the opera house from Warsaw. And I thought it was a joke. No, they were for real. And they would put on a show for us. And this fellow here; he sang me Caruso. "Caruso," I says. Okay, let me here it. Unbelievable. He expanded his chest, and he sang. Oh, beautiful voice. Just unbelievable. They used to say "dumb polock." Don't say that word. I don't believe in that. Every nationality has their own way of living, and every nationality has intelligent people. That's about all I can say. Don't criticize. So we used to have that kind of a show. So one guy says to me,"Benny Goodman." {gurgling sound} Played the clarinet. Unbelievable. They used to remember all the American showmanships they used to have here. Yeah, so. And I don't know if you have anything else you want to ask me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, just right now -- I guess -- free form. Any other vivid memories that come to mind, either about the time before you were captured, or the time in the camp? If you -- anything random comes to mind.

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Yeah, that's where I've been going. Bouncing back and forth.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Think you covered it?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Yeah, pretty well. You know. But probably a lot more. Who knows?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, certainly. It's a lot of --

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: -- Oh, yeah, yeah. It's quite a bit you go through, but there's really a lot more.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, yes. Of course. Exactly. I mean, you can go on and on and on. And you've covered most of the stuff that I talk about, generally. But yeah. Specifically, did you lose any close buddies in that prison camp?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Not in prison.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Before?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: When I was in combat.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How did that happen?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Got shot. They would go on patrol, then they don't come back. Maybe one won't come back. I see him sitting next to me. He's eating, I'm eating. Okay, then we go on patrol. You go on patrol, come back, he's not there. He got shot. So that's tough.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Is that just something you try to put out of your mind?

sp.speaker: Basil Crimaldi
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah. Oh, it comes to you all the time. Oh, yeah, yeah. Especially when you go to bed. You lay there; you got to go to sleep right away because otherwise you'll be up thinking about all that stuff. Keeps going round and round. Always. Never leaves you. Well.
